To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
scintillation camera non-uniformity affects the ability to distinguish between cold lesions and normal organs and tissues.
scintillation camera field nonuniformity has a significant adverse effect on the clinical accuracy of lesion detectability and that this effect is most pronounced in the case of small, cold lesions.
the scintillation camera's nonuniformity, distortion and resolution characteristics have a significant effect on the accuracy of physician readings of cold lesions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of field nonuniformity on the detectability of cold lesions in the scintillation camera.
the effects of scintillation-camera nonuniformities on the detection and diagnosis of cold lesions.
the development of quantitative methods for evaluating the clinical performance of nuclear medicine instrumentation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

nonuniformity is the most critical factor affecting the clinical usefulness of the scintillation camera and that it is the single factor that can most adversely effect the quality of nuclear medicine practice.
the quality of the image produced by a scintillation camera is a function of the quality of the scintillation camera.
the nonuniformity of the gamma camera is an important factor in the clinical interpretation of images and that the nonuniformities must be corrected for by the manufacturer and the user.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nonuniformity, spatial distortion and resolution are important parameters in the evaluation of scintillation cameras.
scintillation camera field uniformity and resolution are the most important factors affecting physician interpretation of clinical images.
scintillation cameras are not a "black box" device and that their performance must be carefully evaluated and documented before use in clinical practice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FDA's current performance standards for scintillation camera non-uniformity are inadequate.

scintillation cameras should be tested for uniformity, distortion and resolution at least once a year, and that these measurements should be made with a phantom containing cold lesions of known size and activity.
nonuniformity correction is critical for the proper use of scintillation cameras in clinical nuclear medicine.
